summary:
Mission Pulse checks each astronaut against their own normal every day, and is built to run on the ship once Earth is too far to help (13 min signal delay at Mars).

How it works: sensors give heart rate, HRV, breathing, skin temperature and sleep. The crew member taps tiredness, stress and mood, plays four short games (vision, hearing, reaction, hand-eye) and does a VR headset session. Each of 11 signals is compared with three personal baselines (Earth normal, space normal, last 7 days) and shown as one of five lights. A transparent model learns per person on board. In our simulated Mars transfer the crew is ready on day 64, 88 days before the delay passes 5 minutes.

VR: one headset, many instruments. It shows each eye its own image in fixed lighting and removes every cue to "up", so one device tests blind spot (SANS), orientation, hand position, self-control, fatigue from blinks, and balance. We designed eight headset tests; three are playable 2D demos. The headset score in the app is simulated for now.

Impact: catches change a population range would miss, separates sensor faults from health problems, and tells non-doctors when to ask for a real test.

Tools: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Kaggle; WESAD data, NASA HERA and Artemis II references, NASA-STD-3001 limits.

Creative: each eye and ear is its own control, and checks are short games crews will actually do. Crew and sensor data are simulated; tests are prototypes, not validated medical tests.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mission Pulse is a daily health check that compares each astronaut with their own normal, and is built to run on the ship once Earth is too far away to help. By the time a crew reaches Mars the one-way signal delay is about 13 minutes, so live help from flight surgeons stops being practical. The crew needs a tool that tells them, in plain terms, who has changed and what to do next.

Every day, sensors supply heart rate, HRV, breathing, skin temperature and sleep. The crew member answers three taps (tiredness, stress, mood), plays four short games, and does a VR headset session. Each of the eleven signals is compared with three personal baselines and shown as one of five lights: no data, act, watch, learning, OK.

THE THREE BASELINES

Every astronaut gets three baselines for every signal. Each is a centre (median) and a spread.

- Earth normal: who you were before launch.

- Space normal: who you are once settled in space. Learned from day 15, then locked. This is the main reference.

- Recent: the last 7 accepted days, not counting today. It catches fast change.

Distances are measured in the person's own day-to-day spread, not a population range. A heart rate of 58 is fine for one astronaut and a warning for another. A one-day blip is yellow. A sudden change on 2 of the last 3 days, or a slow drift lasting 5 days, is red.

THE LEARNING MODEL

Mission Pulse learns a separate model for every astronaut and every signal, on the ship, from that person's own data. It starts from a prior and shifts weight to the person's own data as days build up: with 20 days of heart rate, their own data carries 99.7% of the weight. It uses medians and a robust spread, so one odd day cannot move the baseline. Days more than 3 spreads from normal are kept out of training, so the model never learns illness as normal. The space normal locks after 40 good days that have stayed steady for 14, and a drift check then watches for slow change.

This is personalised anomaly detection. It is a transparent statistical model, not a black box, so every light can be explained to the crew.

THE HANDOVER

A signal counts once its model locks, and the crew is ready when its slowest member is. In our simulated Mars transfer the crew's onboard model is ready on day 64. The signal delay passes 5 minutes on day 152, which leaves an 88-day margin. Everything runs and stores on the ship.

THE GAMES AND THE BIOLOGY BEHIND THEM

- STARSIGHT (vision): in weightlessness, fluid shifts toward the head, the optic nerve swells and the eye flattens (SANS). The game measures contrast sensitivity and near vision, one eye at a time.

- COMMS CHECK (hearing): the station stays near 72 dBA day and night. The game plays spoken digits through static, one ear at a time, so it works in a noisy cabin where a beep test does not.

- ORBIT OPS (reaction): crews sleep about 6 hours against 8.5 scheduled. Round 1 follows the rules of NASA's 3-minute vigilance test.

- DOCKMASTER (hand-eye, memory, attention): the brain re-tunes balance and movement without gravity. Three tasks test memory for order, tracking and a dual task.

VR: ONE HEADSET, MANY INSTRUMENTS

A screen cannot control what each eye sees, how bright the room is, or which way feels like "up". A VR headset can, which makes it the most versatile health instrument a crew can carry. It shows each eye its own image in sealed, fixed lighting, so vision tests stay consistent from day 1 to day 500. It removes every outside cue to "up", so balance and orientation can be tested properly. With eye and hand tracking, the same device also measures visual field, depth judgment, self-control and alertness. That is one piece of hardware doing the work of several, which matters when every kilogram and every minute of crew time counts.

We designed a headset suite of eight tests:

- Blind-Spot Map: each eye maps where a dot vanishes. An enlarged blind spot is an early sign of SANS.

- Lost in the Module: find the right hatch with no fixed "up". Tests orientation and spatial memory, the skill an emergency exit depends on.

- Reach in the Dark: place a target after the lights go out. Tests the sense of hand position, which matters for docking and spacewalks.

- Look Away: look opposite to a flash. Eye tracking scores self-control.

- Blink Alertness: slow blinks and drifting gaze flag fatigue with no extra task for the crew.

- Dual-Task Docking: dock while counting tones. Shows spare mental capacity.

- Which Way Is Up: set a line upright inside a tilted frame. A balance check.

- Each Eye Alone: contrast and sharpness per eye, at fixed distance and light.

Three of these (Lost in the Module, Blink Alertness, Reach in the Dark) are built as playable 2D demos and shown in our slides. Every headset score becomes a daily signal with the same baselines and lights as the rest of the app. In the app today the headset result (a blind-spot score out of 10) is simulated. Running the suite on eye-tracking hardware is our next step.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission Pulse catches change in one person that a population range would miss, tells sensor faults apart from health problems, and shows when the ship can run the monitoring without Earth. Astronauts are not doctors, so no game diagnoses. Each one tells the crew when to ask for the real medical test. The same design fits a spacecraft, a station or a Moon base, because personal baselines keep working however long the mission runs.

TOOLS AND DATA

Python (pygame, numpy), HTML, CSS and JavaScript (canvas, Web Audio), and Kaggle notebooks. The app and the notebooks run the same rules and agree on every flag. Data and references: the WESAD wearable dataset for starting values, NASA's HERA analog habitat and Artemis II as mission references, NASA-STD-3001 for cabin limits, and NASA Human Research Program findings on SANS, sleep and hearing.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Each eye and each ear is its own control: lighting, volume and tiredness affect both sides, so a one-sided change points at the body. Health checks are short games with a story, so crews will actually do them daily. And one headset replaces a shelf of instruments, turning tests that normally need a clinic into a ten-minute session.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

The crew, the sensor data and the headset result are simulated, with planted problems (a short illness, two slow vision declines, a stuck sensor) to test detection. Starting values come from volunteers on Earth, not astronauts. The games and headset tests are prototypes and are not validated medical tests. Two headset tests need eye tracking, which not every headset gives to apps.
